buckets.title: Oscillation foundation: stable equilibrium
buckets.badge_reason: The entry distinction separates return-directed behavior from mere repetition before quantitative oscillator models are used.

capabilities.action: Identify whether a displaced system has a tendency directed back toward one stable equilibrium.
capabilities.success_criterion: Classify a repeated motion by whether displacement to either side produces a return-directed tendency.

capabilities.action: Track how kinetic and potential energy trade through one ideal oscillation cycle while total mechanical energy stays fixed.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify the two kinetic-energy maxima in one displacement cycle and explain why opposite equal displacements carry the same potential-energy state.

microtopics.title: Repetition is not enough: look for a stable equilibrium
microtopics.badge_reason: Repeated motion is visually salient, so learners can miss the stronger requirement that the system's response be organized around one stable equilibrium.
entry_assumptions: Can identify a repeated back-and-forth motion and distinguish position from direction of motion.
microtopics.inferential_jump: An oscillation is organized around a stable equilibrium: when displaced, the system has a tendency that points back toward that equilibrium.

teaching_path.action: Mark one position as the equilibrium and label displacements on opposite sides of it.
teaching_path.why_valid: A return tendency can only be judged relative to a named equilibrium; otherwise back has no fixed destination.

teaching_path.action: Move the same system first to the left of equilibrium and then to the right, recording the direction of its tendency each time.
teaching_path.why_valid: If the equilibrium is stable, the direction must reverse when the side of displacement reverses so that it points inward in both cases.
teaching_path.output: left side -> tendency right; right side -> tendency left

teaching_path.action: Compare that pattern with a motion that repeats around a circular track but has no single position toward which displacement produces a return tendency.
teaching_path.why_valid: The counterexample keeps repetition while removing the stable-equilibrium structure, showing that repetition alone is insufficient.
teaching_path.output: repeats -> yes; one return-directed equilibrium -> no

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any motion that repeats is automatically simple harmonic motion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ball moves periodically around a circular track. Does repetition alone show a restoring tendency toward one equilibrium position?
misconceptions.repair: Separate periodicity from the restoring condition; repetition by itself does not identify simple harmonic motion.

exit_task.prompt: Three motions repeat. For each, decide whether one stable equilibrium organizes the motion and justify the choice by what happens after a displacement to either side.

answer.summary: A qualifying motion has one equilibrium toward which the system tends to return from either side; repetition without that inward pattern is not enough.
reasoning: Name the candidate equilibrium before judging the motion.
Check the response after a displacement on one side and then the other side.
Accept the classification only when the response reverses so that it points toward the same equilibrium from both sides.
answer.check: Swap the side of displacement. A stable equilibrium should make the return tendency swap direction as well; a merely repeating path need not.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task is a qualitative classification of restoring behavior and makes no computed period, frequency or amplitude claim.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created counterexample sequence isolates stable-equilibrium reasoning before any later oscillator equation is admitted.

predict.prompt: If a motion repeats perfectly, is that alone enough to show it is organized around a stable equilibrium?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Repetition can occur without a single position that produces an inward return tendency from both sides.

attempt.produces: A marked equilibrium for each candidate motion, with arrows showing the response after equal displacements to opposite sides.

rubric.criterion: One equilibrium candidate is explicitly marked before arrows are judged.
rubric.evidence_of: Making the reference position part of the reasoning.

rubric.criterion: The response direction is tested on both sides rather than inferred from one example.
rubric.evidence_of: Showing the inward pattern that defines the distinction.

accepted: The sketch marks one center and shows left displacement returning right and right displacement returning left, while the repeating circular case is rejected for lacking that one-center pattern.
rejected: The response accepts every repeating path and never checks what a displacement to the opposite side would make the system do.

task.prompt: You are given two physical systems: (A) a mass on a spring stretched from its natural length, and (B) a ball rolling along the inside of a circular loop. For each, propose one candidate equilibrium position. Then displace the system slightly to the left of that position and describe the direction of its tendency. Repeat for a displacement to the right. State whether each system passes the two-sided stable-equilibrium test.
givens: System A: ideal spring; natural-length position is the candidate equilibrium.
System B: ideal frictionless circular loop; consider the lowest point as the candidate equilibrium.

route.ask: Where would you place one position that the system could be displaced away from?
route.why_this_ask: A return tendency is meaningless until the learner proposes an equilibrium.

route.ask: After moving the system to the left of that point, which way would a return tendency have to point?
route.why_this_ask: The first side gives a concrete directional prediction.

route.ask: Now move it to the other side. What must reverse if the same point is truly stable?
route.why_this_ask: The second side tests whether the result is structural rather than accidental.

route.ask: Can a circular repeating path pass the same two-sided test?
route.why_this_ask: The counterexample removes stable equilibrium while preserving repetition.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path contrasts examples directly; the elicitation route makes the learner nominate an equilibrium and commit to two opposite-side predictions before seeing the counterexample.

boundary_test.prompt: If the system is placed exactly at the stable equilibrium and left undisturbed, which return direction should be preferred?
boundary_test.answer: Neither side should be preferred; the defining return-direction test begins after a displacement away from equilibrium.
boundary_test.confirms: The concept concerns response to displacement around an equilibrium, not a permanent arrow attached at the center.

independent_checks.statement: Swap the displacement to the opposite side. A stable equilibrium must reverse the tendency direction.
Test a system that repeats without a single stable equilibrium (e.g., circular track) to confirm the criterion is not trivially satisfied by repetition alone.

compact_anchor.prompt: A ball in a bowl is displaced to the left. What direction is its tendency? Displaced to the right?
compact_anchor.result: Left: tendency points right (toward bottom). Right: tendency points left (toward bottom). Both inward → stable equilibrium → qualifies as oscillation.

microtopics.title: Energy trades twice during one displacement cycle
microtopics.badge_reason: The position cycle repeats once while the energy pattern repeats at both center crossings, so learners must coordinate two time patterns without confusing sign with stored energy.
entry_assumptions: Can identify turning points and equilibrium crossings in a repeated back-and-forth motion.
Can read a quantity as nonnegative even when position lies on the negative side of equilibrium.
microtopics.inferential_jump: In an ideal oscillator, energy shifts between motion and displacement storage while the total stays fixed; the energy state is the same at equal-magnitude displacements on opposite sides, so the kinetic-potential pattern repeats twice during one full displacement cycle.

teaching_path.action: Mark five ordered checkpoints for one full displacement cycle: positive turning point, center crossing, negative turning point, second center crossing, and return to the positive turning point.
teaching_path.why_valid: The energy pattern can only be counted against a complete position cycle if the cycle's repeated geometric checkpoints are fixed first.

teaching_path.action: Assign the dominant energy form at each checkpoint while keeping the same total mechanical-energy level across the row.
teaching_path.why_valid: At turning points the instantaneous motion is absent while displacement storage is greatest; at center crossings the displacement storage is least while motion is greatest.
teaching_path.output: turn: KE low / PE high ; center: KE high / PE low ; turn: KE low / PE high ; center: KE high / PE low

teaching_path.action: Compare the positive and negative turning points, then count the center crossings before the displacement pattern returns to its start.
teaching_path.why_valid: Opposite equal-magnitude displacements produce the same energy state, so sign reversal does not make stored energy negative; two center crossings give two kinetic-energy maxima per position cycle.
teaching_path.output: +turn energy state = -turn energy state ; 1 displacement cycle -> 2 KE maxima

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Potential energy becomes negative whenever displacement is on the negative side of equilibrium.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At equal distances on opposite sides of equilibrium, should the ideal oscillator have different stored-energy amounts just because one position has a negative sign?
misconceptions.repair: Treat the side of equilibrium and the stored-energy amount separately: opposite equal-magnitude displacements have the same potential-energy state.

exit_task.prompt: Follow one ideal oscillation from a positive turning point back to the same turning point. How many times does kinetic energy reach a maximum, and why does the total mechanical energy not rise and fall with those maxima?

answer.summary: Kinetic energy reaches a maximum twice, once at each equilibrium crossing, while the total mechanical energy stays constant because kinetic and potential energy exchange rather than being created or destroyed.
reasoning: One full displacement cycle crosses equilibrium twice before returning to the starting turning point.
Each center crossing is the state of greatest motion and least displacement storage, so kinetic energy peaks at both crossings.
At the turning points the balance reverses; the changing shares add to the same total throughout the ideal cycle.
answer.check: Lay the energy sequence under the five position checkpoints; the first and last energy states must match, and the two center checkpoints must carry the two kinetic-energy maxima.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer gives a qualitative cycle count and conservation explanation; it computes no energy value, frequency, or oscillator parameter.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created checkpoint sequence teaches the double-repeat energy pattern and sign-independent stored-energy distinction without introducing an ungated oscillator energy equation.

predict.prompt: During one complete back-and-forth position cycle, do you expect kinetic energy to peak once or more than once?
predict.defensible_answer: It peaks twice, because the oscillator passes through equilibrium twice before returning to the starting turning point.

attempt.produces: A five-checkpoint position row with kinetic and potential energy marked high or low at each checkpoint and one constant-total line beneath it.

rubric.criterion: Both equilibrium crossings are marked as kinetic-energy maxima.
rubric.evidence_of: Coordinating the energy pattern with the full displacement cycle rather than counting only half a cycle.

rubric.criterion: Opposite turning points are assigned the same stored-energy state and the total is kept fixed.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating position sign from energy sign and applying ideal mechanical-energy conservation.

accepted: The row shows high kinetic energy at both center crossings, high potential energy at both turning points, and one unchanged total across all five checkpoints.
rejected: The negative turning point is assigned negative potential energy and only one center crossing is counted before the cycle is declared complete.

task.prompt: An ideal spring-mass system is displaced 10 cm to the right of equilibrium and released from rest. Fill in a five-row table with columns: Checkpoint | KE (HIGH/LOW) | PE (HIGH/LOW) | E_total (constant?). Checkpoints in order: right turn, centre, left turn, centre, right turn. Then state how many times KE is HIGH in one cycle.
givens: Released from rest at 10 cm to the right of equilibrium.
At a turning point: instantaneous speed is zero.
At equilibrium crossing: displacement is zero.

route.ask: What ordered checkpoints must you pass before the displacement pattern has truly returned to its starting state?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must define a complete cycle before counting energy events.

route.ask: At a turning point, which energy share is largest and which is smallest?
route.why_this_ask: This anchors the energy bookkeeping at a state with no instantaneous motion.

route.ask: How many center crossings occur before the position cycle closes, and what energy event occurs at each?
route.why_this_ask: This produces the twice-per-cycle pattern from the motion rather than stating it.

route.ask: Why should the two opposite turning points have the same stored-energy state?
route.why_this_ask: The final ask directly tests the misconception that negative position implies negative stored energy.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path lays out the five checkpoints before assigning energy; the elicitation route makes the learner define the cycle boundary and discover the repeated energy state by counting crossings.

boundary_test.prompt: If mechanical energy is lost to an external dissipative interaction, should the constant-total row still be used unchanged?
boundary_test.answer: No. The constant-total claim belongs to the ideal oscillator case; with an energy-losing interaction the mechanical total can decrease.
boundary_test.confirms: The conservation statement is tied to the ideal model rather than asserted for every real oscillation.

independent_checks.statement: Check that the energy states at the two turning points are equal (opposite equal-magnitude displacements → same PE).
Confirm two centre crossings are recorded before the displacement pattern completes one cycle; if only one is recorded, the cycle boundary was drawn too early.

compact_anchor.prompt: How many times does kinetic energy reach its maximum value in one complete back-and-forth displacement cycle of an ideal oscillator?
compact_anchor.result: Twice — once at each of the two equilibrium crossings during the cycle. Opposite turning points carry the same potential energy (equal magnitudes), so kinetic energy peaks symmetrically.

relations.expression: F_restoring has opposite sign to displacement x for stable equilibrium
relations.meaning: At a stable equilibrium the net tendency on the system when displaced by x has the opposite sign to the displacement: displacement left produces tendency right, and vice versa.

symbols.meaning: Net restoring tendency on the displaced system

conditions: The system must be displaced and released to test the relation.
Holds for small displacements in the linear restoring-force regime.

derivation.action: Mark the equilibrium position and define positive and negative displacement.
derivation.why_valid: Sign convention must precede directional comparison.
derivation.output: x = 0 at equilibrium; left is negative, right is positive (or declared axis)

derivation.action: Displace to +x: record tendency direction. Displace to -x: record tendency direction.
derivation.why_valid: Stable equilibrium requires the tendency to point inward from both sides.
derivation.output: F_net · x < 0 at both test displacements

limits: The relation characterises the qualitative stability condition, not a specific force law.
Quantitative SHM kinematics (period, frequency, amplitude) are outside this relation.
checks: Swap displacement direction; the tendency direction must swap.

relations.expression: KE + PE = E_total (constant) for ideal oscillator
relations.meaning: In an ideal oscillator, kinetic and potential energy exchange while their sum remains fixed: KE is maximum at equilibrium crossings and zero at turning points; PE has the opposite pattern. The two equilibrium crossings per displacement cycle give two KE maxima.

symbols.meaning: Instantaneous potential energy stored by the restoring mechanism
Total mechanical energy (constant in ideal case)

conditions: No energy is lost to dissipation.
PE depends on displacement magnitude, not direction, so opposite equal displacements carry the same PE.

derivation.action: Mark five checkpoints in one displacement cycle: +turn, centre, -turn, centre, +turn.
derivation.why_valid: A complete cycle must return to its starting state.

derivation.action: Assign dominant energy form at each checkpoint.
derivation.why_valid: At turns: speed zero → KE=0; at centre: displacement zero → PE=0.
derivation.output: T: PE high/KE low; C: KE high/PE low; total unchanged

limits: Does not specify SHM kinematics, period, or amplitude.
checks: Two centre crossings per cycle → two KE maxima per cycle. Verify both are recorded.

representations.title: Oscillation cycle position-and-energy diagram
representations.description: A five-checkpoint position row with arrows indicating return tendency and KE/PE labels.

question_families.title: Classify oscillatory motion by the two-sided stable-equilibrium test
solution_structure: Test the response tendency from a displacement to the left.
Test the response tendency from a displacement to the right.
Accept if both tendencies point inward toward the same equilibrium.

question_families.title: Track kinetic-potential energy exchange through one ideal oscillation cycle
solution_structure: Mark five ordered checkpoints for one complete displacement cycle.
Classify KE and PE as HIGH or LOW at each checkpoint.
Verify that opposite turning points share the same PE.
Count the two KE maxima; confirm total energy is constant.

demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Position cycle to energy ledger table.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Checkpoint, energy assignment, count KE maxima, verify total.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Non-ideal (dissipative) cases or unequal turning-point magnitudes vary the demand.

safe_variations: Change the oscillator type (pendulum, spring); change starting position.
transfer_boundaries: Does not cover quantitative energy values, SHM equations or wave propagation.
common_wrong_routes: Counting only one KE maximum; assigning negative PE to a negative displacement.

questions.stem: A ball on a curved bowl repeatedly moves back and forth. (a) Mark the equilibrium position. (b) Describe the direction of the ball's tendency when displaced to the left and when displaced to the right of equilibrium. (c) Does this motion qualify as oscillation? Justify using the two-sided tendency test.
conditions: Ideal frictionless bowl; repeated back-and-forth motion observed.

answer.summary: Yes, it qualifies. The bottom of the bowl is the equilibrium; displaced left → tendency right; displaced right → tendency left.
reasoning: (a) The lowest point of the bowl is the equilibrium: released there with no speed, the ball stays.
(b) Left displacement: gravity component points rightward toward the bottom; right displacement: gravity component points leftward toward the bottom.
(c) Both sides produce an inward tendency toward the same equilibrium, satisfying the two-sided test. This is oscillatory motion organized around a stable equilibrium.
answer.check: The tendency direction must reverse when the side of displacement reverses; the circular-track counterexample would fail this test.

subpart_answers.value: Left → tendency right; right → tendency left
Yes; inward tendency from both sides confirms stable equilibrium.

difficulty.basis: Applies stable-equilibrium two-sided test to a simple bowl-and-ball system.

questions.stem: An ideal pendulum is released from rest at its rightmost position. Using five ordered checkpoints (right turn, centre, left turn, centre, right turn), classify kinetic energy as HIGH or LOW and potential energy as HIGH or LOW at each checkpoint. How many times does kinetic energy reach a maximum in one complete displacement cycle?
conditions: Ideal (no friction); released from rest at rightmost turning point.

answer.summary: KE peaks twice per cycle (at both centre crossings). Total energy stays constant.
reasoning: Right turn: speed = 0 (turning point) → KE LOW, PE HIGH.
Centre (going left): maximum speed → KE HIGH, PE LOW.
Left turn: speed = 0 → KE LOW, PE HIGH.
Centre (going right): maximum speed → KE HIGH, PE LOW.
Right turn: back to KE LOW, PE HIGH.
KE is HIGH at both centre checkpoints → 2 maxima per displacement cycle.
Total = KE + PE remains unchanged at every checkpoint (ideal oscillator).
answer.check: The right and left turning points must have the same PE (equal magnitude displacements → same stored energy); the two centre crossings must share the same KE.

difficulty.basis: Applies five-checkpoint energy ledger to an ideal pendulum; no computation.

questions.stem: Three motions are described: (P) A mass on a spring bouncing vertically. (Q) A planet orbiting a star in a circular path. (R) A ball in a bowl tilted so the surface curves upward on one side and downward on the other. Apply the two-sided stable-equilibrium test to each. Classify P, Q, R as oscillatory (organized around a stable equilibrium) or not.
conditions: Apply only the two-sided inward-tendency test; do not appeal to quantitative formulas.

answer.summary: P: oscillatory. Q: not oscillatory by this test. R: not oscillatory (no single stable equilibrium).
reasoning: P: Spring mass — compressed (above equilibrium) gives downward tendency; stretched (below) gives upward tendency. Both inward → stable equilibrium. Oscillatory.

Q: Circular orbit — displacement from the circular path does not produce a tendency that returns the planet to the same one equilibrium position. The orbit has no single return point. Not oscillatory by this test.

R: Asymmetric bowl — on the side that curves upward the ball returns; on the side that curves downward the ball continues away. The tendency is inward from one side only, not both. No single stable equilibrium. Not oscillatory.
answer.check: Confirm each decision by checking the other side: P reverses direction from both sides; Q and R do not pass from both sides.

hints.text: For each case, propose one position as the candidate equilibrium and test what happens on both sides.
Reject any case where the tendency does not point inward from both displacement directions.
P: oscillatory. Q: not. R: not.

questions.failure_signal: If you classified Q (circular orbit) as oscillatory, check whether the orbital path has one equilibrium position that produces an inward return tendency from both displacement directions.

family_exposure.closure: You applied the two-sided stable-equilibrium test to three systems, correctly accepted one, and rejected two with distinct failure modes.

difficulty.basis: Multi-case stable-equilibrium classification requiring explicit two-sided test with one non-obvious rejection (circular orbit).

questions.stem: An ideal pendulum is released from 5 cm to the right of equilibrium. A thin layer of air resistance then slows it gradually. (a) For the first complete swing (before significant energy loss), fill in a five-checkpoint energy table as in the ideal case. (b) After many swings, the amplitude has halved to 2.5 cm. State whether the energy state at the (new, smaller) turning points is the same HIGH/LOW classification as before. Explain why the total mechanical energy must have decreased. (c) A student says "The total energy can never change in a pendulum." Identify the specific assumption that makes this claim false here.
conditions: Part (a): use the ideal-oscillator model for the first swing.
Part (b): air resistance has removed energy over many swings.
Qualitative reasoning only; no numerical energy values required.

answer.summary: (a) Standard ideal table. (b) PE at turning points is now lower (smaller amplitude); total decreased. (c) The claim requires "no energy-removing interaction", violated by air resistance.
reasoning: (a) +T: KE LOW, PE HIGH; Centre: KE HIGH, PE LOW; −T: KE LOW, PE HIGH; Centre: KE HIGH, PE LOW; +T: KE LOW, PE HIGH. Total constant at each checkpoint.

(b) Smaller amplitude means smaller displacement at the turning points → less stored PE at each turning point. Classification is still PE HIGH / KE LOW at turning points, but the HIGH level is now lower than before. The total mechanical energy has decreased because air resistance converted some mechanical energy to heat over the many swings.

(c) The claim "total energy never changes" assumes no dissipative interaction. Air resistance is precisely such an interaction; it removes mechanical energy and transfers it to the surrounding air as thermal energy.
answer.check: Confirm that the ideal table from (a) uses the constant-total assumption; (b) shows that constant-total fails when a dissipative interaction is present.

subpart_answers.value: Five-row table: turns = KE LOW / PE HIGH; centres = KE HIGH / PE LOW; E_total constant.
Still HIGH/LOW classification at turning points, but HIGH PE is smaller; total mechanical energy decreased.
The assumption is "no energy-losing interaction." Air resistance violates this; it converts mechanical energy to heat.

rubric.criterion: Ideal five-checkpoint table is correctly completed.
Recognises that amplitude loss means less stored PE at turning points.
Identifies that constant-total requires no dissipation.
rubric.evidence_of: The boundary condition of the ideal model.

reasoning_route.action: Smaller amplitude → smaller turning-point displacement → less PE at turns.
reasoning_route.output: PE HIGH but lower than before

reasoning_route.action: Total decreased because air resistance converted energy to heat.
The claim requires no dissipative interaction; air resistance violates this.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The ideal model assumption is explicit.

adaptation.reason: Air resistance introduces a non-ideal dissipative interaction; the learner must apply the ideal model for one swing, then diagnose why the constant-total claim breaks down over many swings.

hints.text: Part (a) uses the ideal model: apply the five-checkpoint table as practised.
For part (b): smaller turning-point displacement means less stored PE; total mechanical energy can only stay constant with no losses.
(a) Standard table. (b) Total decreased due to air resistance. (c) Air resistance violates no-dissipation assumption.

questions.failure_signal: If you said the total energy stays the same despite air resistance, you are applying the ideal-oscillator assumption to a non-ideal case. The boundary test in the Core1A material explicitly states that constant-total does not hold when a dissipative interaction is present.

family_exposure.closure: You applied the ideal energy ledger to one swing, recognized that dissipation breaks the constant-total assumption, and identified the specific assumption violated.

transfer.statement: Air resistance makes the oscillator non-ideal; the five-checkpoint ideal table still applies for the first swing, but over many swings the amplitude decreases and the total mechanical energy falls.
transfer.invariant: At each turning point KE is LOW and PE is HIGH; at each equilibrium crossing KE is HIGH and PE is LOW. The two KE maxima per cycle pattern persists even in the dissipating case.

novelty.why_new: Q-OSC-1A-ENERGY-01 (Core1A anchor) uses an ideal oscillator where E_total is constant by construction. No earlier item introduces a dissipative interaction that changes E_total over time. No earlier item asks the learner to apply the ideal model for one swing and then diagnose why it fails over many swings. The claim-identification demand in part (c) is genuinely new: it requires the learner to name the exact assumption (no dissipation) that the student's claim requires, which no prior Core1A or Core2A item tests.

difficulty.basis: Ideal-to-non-ideal boundary: applies ideal model for one swing, diagnoses assumption failure over many swings, identifies violated model condition.

learner_actions: Read the completed two-sided equilibrium test.

help_plan: Ask for the equilibrium before naming the rule.
Delay the circular counterexample until both side predictions are committed.
Close with the exact boundary at equilibrium.
